# The Heat Is Unequal: How Cities Can Make Summer More Bearable

Summer in the city has always been hotter than summer in the countryside, but climate change has transformed a familiar discomfort into a genuine public health crisis. Urban heat islands—the phenomenon whereby cities run several degrees warmer than surrounding areas—now kill more Americans annually than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined. The built environment is largely to blame: asphalt absorbs solar radiation, buildings block cooling breezes, air conditioners pump waste heat into streets, and the scarcity of vegetation removes both shade and the evaporative cooling that plants provide. The good news is that cities are not condemned to swelter. Through deliberate choices about trees, street design, housing, and public transit, urban leaders can dramatically reduce the dangers of extreme heat. The catch, as with any public investment, is that these choices involve tradeoffs—and those tradeoffs are rarely distributed evenly.

## Trees: The Oldest and Best Air Conditioner

The single most effective intervention against urban heat is also the most ancient: shade. A mature street tree can lower the perceived temperature beneath its canopy by as much as 20 to 25 degrees Fahrenheit, transforming a dangerous sidewalk into a walkable one.
